name: Bissa, Barka dialect

catalog_quote: When asked, most Bissa speakers will say that Bissa has three tones, and cite the following minimal triplet as proof: [gɛ́r] ‘someone’ [gɛ̄r] ‘road’ [gɛ̀r] ‘stone’ In the existing documents discussing Bissa however, there is a wide range of opinion regarding the tone system. In his grammar of the Lebri dialect, Anthony Naden doesn’t address the question of tone. Where he does come close to discussing tone, he refers to it as intonation and simply states that “There is very little use of suprasegmental phonological features in the Syntax of Bisa.” (Naden 1973: 244) This lack of treatment of tone has led some people to conclude that Bissa is a toneless language – see for instance the posting for Bissa on WALS. Schreiber suggests that Bissa may be a pitch-accent language, rather than a tonal language (Schreiber 2000: 60). ... We therefore conclude, as did Galbane, that Bissa Barka has two level tones, H and L and four tone melodiesː H, HL, L and LH. ... In summary, our study on the tone in the personal pronouns in Bissa Barka has revealed that Bissa Barka has two underlying level tones, H and L that combine to create four tone melodies: H, L, LH and HL. These four melodies behave in distinct ways. We have observed four tonal processes: 1. LH is realized as L 2. Final L tones fall 3. L tone spread 4. Restriction on L + L

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bissa is a tone language: two level tones H and L, distributed over the word as one of four word melodies (H, HL, L, LH) regardless of syllable count; a mid tone perceived by speakers is the surface realisation of the LH melody in isolation. No source opened says where word stress falls; the only remarks on non-tonal prominence are second-hand (Naden 1973 saw little use of suprasegmentals; Schreiber 2000 floated a pitch accent analysis, which Morris does not adopt).
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned in any opened source
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal processes only: LH realised as L in isolation, final L falls, L-tone spread, restriction on L+L; earlier authors disagree on 2 vs 3 tones (Prost 1950, Zouré 1975, Bambara 1980, Monet 1989 three tones; Hidden 1982, Galbane 1985, Vanhoudt 1992, Morris 2016 two tones plus downstep/melodies). WALS 13A codes Bisa 'No tones' from Naden 1973, which Morris rejects.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone melodies on simple nouns and verbs elicited in isolation and in short phrases (250 items, Garango speakers), then pronouns in clauses and possessive phrases; Barka dialect. Vanhoudt's Lebir (Zabré) data use H, B and H-abaissé tones.
new_statements.identity_note: Morris 2016 describes the Barka dialect as spoken in Garango (Glottolog bark1245 'Barka (Burkina Faso)'); the Vanhoudt items describe the Lebir dialect of Zabré (lebi1240 Lebir / lere1242 Lere). The two dialects are reported as mutually unintelligible (Vanhoudt 1992: 83) but both are analysed as two-tone systems by their best sources. Glottolog's listing of Wood 2014 'Categorial Grammars' under biss1248 is a misattribution (not about Bissa).

new_statements.quote: [p. 86] B. LES TONS. 1. TONALITE VOCALIQUE. Toute voyelle porte au moins un ton. Le bisa possède trois tons ponctuels: haut [á], bas [à], abaissé [ā], et cinq tons mélodiques: bas-haut, haut-bas, haut-abaissé, abaissé-bas et bas-haut-bas. [...] [p. 92] SYNTHESE. Nos données attestent la présence de trois tonèmes: haut, bas et abaissé. [...] En résumé, trois tonèmes - haut, bas et abaissé - se réalisent sur le plan phonétique par trois tons simples (haut, bas, abaissé) et six tons complexes ou modulés lorsqu'ils forment une séquence tonale associée à une même syllabe. [...] [intro, PDF p. 10] Les travaux de Prost et de Naden envisagent de nombreux aspects de la langue mais ignorent le système tonal, pourtant essentiel tant sur le plan lexical que morphosyntaxique.
new_statements.translation: [p. 86] B. TONES. 1. Vowel tonality. Every vowel bears at least one tone. Bisa has three level tones: high, low, downstepped ('abaissé'), and five contour tones: low-high, high-low, high-downstepped, downstepped-low and low-high-low. [...] [p. 92] Synthesis. Our data attest three tonemes: high, low and downstepped. [...] In sum, three tonemes - high, low and downstepped - are realised phonetically as three simple tones and six complex or contour tones when they form a tonal sequence associated with one syllable. [...] [intro] The works of Prost and Naden treat many aspects of the language but ignore the tonal system, which is essential both lexically and morphosyntactically.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog classification tonal (Morris 2016) and with the existing statement 'tone language, no stress statement': a 500-page grammar whose suprasegmental chapters are entirely about tone and which never mentions word stress. Two differences of detail, not of kind: (i) dialect — Vanhoudt describes Lebir (Zabré), the catalog item names Barka (Garango); (ii) tone inventory — Vanhoudt posits three tonemes (H, L, downstepped H) for Lebir where Morris 2016 concludes two level tones plus four melodies for Barka (Morris p. 78 already reviews this range of opinion). Vanhoudt's introduction also independently confirms Morris's remark that Naden 1973 and Prost 1950 do not treat tone, wh…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The thesis analyses Bisa (Lebir dialect of Zabré) as a tone language with three tonemes (H, L and a phonemic downstepped H 'abaissé', never utterance-initial), realised as three level and six contour tones, with tone-bearing syllabic nasals after pause, assertive-sentence downdrift, lexical tone schemes for nouns and verbs (L-initial schemes dominant) and 24 morphotonological rules (tone spreading, floating tones). It contains no section and no statement on word stress or accent: the only occurrences of 'accent-' in the 618 pages are 'cet effet downdrift.. peut s'accentuer sur la dernière syllabe' (p. 91, about intonation) and 'mettre l'accent sur' (p. 400, idiom). Suprasegmental phonology = tone only.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (no stress discussed at all)
new_statements.exceptions: none regarding stress; for tone: the downstepped toneme cannot occur utterance-initially or after L/HL; HB and BH schemes on short unchecked vowels essentially unattested; many idiolectal tonal variants (informants FG, GS, SDM).
new_statements.identity_note: Vanhoudt 1992 describes the Lebir dialect of Bisa as spoken at Zabré (southern edge of the Bisa area, Boulgou province, Burkina Faso), from Zabré-born informants recorded 1983-1991; the catalog item is named for the Barka dialect (Garango). Glottolog biss1248 covers both (dialects bark1245 Barka, lebi1240 Lebir).

sources.note: Sect. 2 'Levels of tone' (pp. 77-81) and Conclusion (p. 91): Bissa Barka has two level tones H and L combining into four word melodies H, HL, L, LH (established by a 250-word card-sort with speakers of Garango). No statement on word stress; reports second-hand that Naden 1973: 244 found 'very little use of suprasegmental phonological features in the Syntax of Bisa' and that Schreiber 2000: 60 'suggests that Bissa may be a pitch accent language, rather than a tonal language'; rejects the WALS 'no tones' coding.
